subtype: Approach: picks the plan that fits what matters most to them [Thinking]
passage:
Note, Friday, Class 4. Eshaan came to me at break holding two invitations, one in each hand. One was for a classmate's cricket-match party on Saturday, and the other was for Nani's birthday lunch at the same hour. I asked only, "Which one are you thinking about?" Eshaan said, "The match has a real bat and ball and a cake." Then he went quiet. "But Nani is seventy this year and she will keep asking where I am. There will be other matches. There are not many seventieth birthdays." He put the party card in his bag and said he would tell his friend on Monday. I asked whether he was sure. He nodded. I did not say what I would choose.

Madhuri, class teacher

qa.q: How old is Nani this year?
qa.a: Nani is seventy this year.

qa.q: What did Eshaan want when he said Nani would keep asking where he was?
qa.a: Eshaan wanted to be with Nani, because he cared about her and thought she would miss him more than the match would.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do to keep his friend happy?
qa.a: Eshaan could explain kindly on Monday and ask to play cricket with the friend on another day.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Eshaan arrives at the lunch?
qa.a: Nani might feel happy and loved, since Eshaan chose to be with her.

grounding: Shows a boy weighing two invitations aloud and choosing the family birthday because it matters more to him than the match.

subtype: Approach: names what matters before choosing a path [Thinking]
passage: Ishita, sit. Suresh was sixteen once and had two doors in front of me: a coaching class that promised a good rank, or a music course with a teacher I liked. Everyone said rank. So I took a sheet of paper and wrote first, not the names of the courses, but what I wanted from my life: to make things, and to decide my own days. Creativity. Independence. Then I put each course beside those two words. Coaching gave me a timetable made by someone else. Music gave me a violin and a choice. I showed the page to Papa and Ma at dinner. Papa said, "Good. Now let's check whether the fees and the travel are workable." Ma asked me to try one month of music first. We agreed. The list did not choose for me. It showed me what I was choosing.

qa.q: Which two values did Suresh write on the page?
qa.a: Suresh wrote creativity and independence.

qa.q: What did Suresh want from life, according to the story?
qa.a: Suresh wanted to make things and to decide the days, which is why a timetable made by someone else felt wrong.

qa.q: Which step in the story made the choice clearer, and why?
qa.a: Writing the values before naming the courses let Suresh hold each course up against them.

qa.q: How might Ma have felt about trying one month of music first?
qa.a: Ma may have felt cautious but supportive, wanting Suresh to try the music course while keeping a chance to review it.

grounding: Shows a student naming what matters before choosing between a coaching class and a music course, with parents' input.

subtype: Approach: checks each option against a short list of personal values [Action]
passage:
'Two offers,' Deepak said, dropping onto Vaibhav's bed. 'Startup A: sixty hours a week, unpaid, and they said "we'll see about a job later". Startup B: thirty hours, a small stipend, and a mentor.'

'Sixty? But A is the big name.'

'Last month I wrote three words on my wall. Honesty. Learning. Family time.' Deepak pointed at the paper. 'So I'm asking each offer the same three questions.'

'And?'

'A: their ad says flexible hours and it isn't, so honesty, no. Learning, maybe, but nobody would teach me. Family time, zero. Sunday lunch is gone.'

'And B?'

'B fits all three.'

'So you'll say no to A?'

'Already typed the email.'

qa.q: Which three values did Deepak write on the wall?
qa.a: Deepak wrote honesty, learning and family time.

qa.q: How does Deepak feel about turning down Startup A?
qa.a: Deepak feels settled and sure, since the email was already typed.

qa.q: What could Deepak do if Startup B also starts asking for more hours?
qa.a: Deepak could ask the same three questions again and talk to the mentor about limits before agreeing.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see Deepak's approach?
qa.a: Vaibhav may find it surprising since A is the big name, but may respect that Deepak used clear reasons.

grounding: Shows a student testing internship offers against a short list of values and refusing the one that would erode them.

subtype: Approach: follows a stated value without checking real constraints [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Nikita,

You asked how the village work is going. Truthfully, it has not started. In March I quit my job the same day I decided to. I had no savings to speak of and no organisation waiting, only the certainty that I should be helping village schools. Part of my salary paid the rent at my parents' place and my brother's college fees, and I had never sat down and worked that out. Within six weeks I was applying to offices again. What I wanted to do was never wrong. I skipped the part where I check who depends on me. I am ashamed to write this, but I would rather you heard it from me.

Dolma

qa.q: In which month did Dolma quit the job?
qa.a: Dolma quit the job in March.

qa.q: How does Dolma feel while writing this email?
qa.a: Dolma feels ashamed but wants to be honest with Nikita.

qa.q: What could Dolma have done before quitting?
qa.a: Dolma could have listed who depends on the income, found an organisation or part-time route first, and moved in steps.

qa.q: How might Dolma's parents have been affected?
qa.a: Dolma's parents may have been worried, since the rent and the brother's fees depended partly on the salary.

grounding: Shows a professional following a sound value by quitting with no savings or plan, ignoring family obligations.

subtype: Approach: keeps the value and rebuilds the route in stages [Revision]
passage:
Payal sat with Akash, her old manager, in the office canteen. "I quit too fast last time," she said. "I still want to work with village clinics. That hasn't changed."

Akash asked how she would go about it this time.

"In stages. First, part-time here, three days a week. Second, saving for a year so my parents' expenses stay covered. Third, weekends with the rural health group, doing whatever help they need: registers, bookings, driving."

"And then?"

"After a year I decide whether to move over fully, based on what I actually see."

Akash nodded. "Sounds slow."

"It is," said Payal. "But I'm still going in the same direction."

qa.q: How many days a week will Payal work part-time?
qa.a: Payal will work part-time three days a week.

qa.q: How does Payal seem to feel about her earlier decision?
qa.a: Payal seems regretful but still determined, since she says she quit too fast but still wants the work.

qa.q: What could Payal check during the year of volunteering?
qa.a: Payal could check whether the work suits her day to day, and whether money and family needs can be covered if she moves over fully.

qa.q: How might Akash see Payal's new plan?
qa.a: Akash may feel reassured, seeing Payal keep her aim while taking slow steps.

grounding: Shows a person keeping her value and rebuilding the route in stages, working part-time and volunteering before a bigger shift.

subtype: Approach: goes to a calm spot when upset before trying again [Action]
passage:
Monday. Reyansh pushed the puzzle away and it slid off the table. "It doesn't fit!" His face was hot. Mama Jaya said, "Come and sit with me." He climbed onto her lap and breathed with her until his shoulders came down.

Tuesday. The puzzle came out again. When a piece would not fit, Reyansh's lip shook. He got up by himself, went to Mama on the sofa and sat quietly for a while. Then he went back to the table.

Wednesday. Reyansh finished the corner, and a picture of a fish showed. "I sat first," he told Mama.

qa.q: What picture showed in the puzzle?
qa.a: A picture of a fish showed.

qa.q: How did Reyansh feel when the piece did not fit on Monday?
qa.a: Reyansh felt frustrated and angry, since his face was hot and he pushed the puzzle away.

qa.q: What could Mama do if Reyansh still gets upset next time?
qa.a: Mama could stay close and help with one piece, or suggest a smaller puzzle so that he can succeed.

qa.q: How might Mama feel on seeing Reyansh come to sit by himself on Tuesday?
qa.a: Mama might feel proud and glad that Reyansh knows how to calm down.

grounding: Shows a child pushing away a puzzle in frustration, sitting with his mother until calmer and returning to try again.

subtype: Approach: picks an easier task when tired or upset [Thinking]
passage: I am Ayesha, and I had my science test tomorrow. My tummy felt fizzy and my head felt full. When I opened my book, the words swam. I thought, if I start now I will only cry. So I took my colour pencils and drew my favourite thing, a big elephant with a red hat. I drew for ten minutes and did not think about the test at all. My shoulders came down. Then I closed the drawing book and read the first chapter. It was easier, because my mind was quiet. Deepak, my brother, saw the elephant and said it looked funny. I said, "I know. It helped."

qa.q: What did Ayesha draw?
qa.a: Ayesha drew a big elephant with a red hat.

qa.q: How was Ayesha feeling before the test?
qa.a: Ayesha was worried, with a fizzy tummy and a full head.

qa.q: What else could Ayesha do if drawing does not help Ayesha calm down?
qa.a: Ayesha could ask Deepak or a parent to sit close for a few minutes, or take a short walk before starting.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen Ayesha's drawing time?
qa.a: Deepak thought the elephant looked funny, and may have understood that it was a way of calming down.

grounding: Shows a child doing a favourite drawing for ten minutes to calm down before starting to revise.

subtype: Approach: schedules hard work at the times of day when energy is highest [Action]
passage:
Dear Pranav,

You asked how I am finding time for maths. Here is the trick I stumbled on. Last month I kept a little tally: at night my sums took forever and I made silly mistakes, but at six in the morning they came fast. So now I wake at 5:45, do maths for an hour with a cup of tea, and the hardest thing of my day is done. In the evening I only read my Hindi and history notes, or a novel for twenty minutes, because my brain is tired then and that is fine. I have done this for two weeks and I no longer dread Tuesday's maths class. Try tracking when you feel sharpest. See you at cricket on Sunday!

Imran

qa.q: At what time does Imran wake up?
qa.a: Imran wakes at 5:45.

qa.q: How does Imran feel about maths class now?
qa.a: Imran feels less afraid, since Tuesday's maths class is no longer dreaded.

qa.q: What could Imran do if a family event stops the early mornings?
qa.a: Imran could move the maths hour to another clear time and check whether the mistakes stay low.

qa.q: How might Pranav see the advice?
qa.a: Pranav might be curious and try tracking the hours that feel sharpest.

grounding: Shows Imran noticing that early mornings suit the hardest thinking and putting maths then, with lighter work in the evening.

subtype: Approach: makes big decisions while angry or anxious [Pitfall]
passage:
Urmila: You once told me you almost left engineering. What happened?

Vasudev: The mechanics result came out and I had failed. My friends were all fine. I walked home shaking, opened the transfer form and filled it in that same night. All I could think was: everyone has seen it, I'm the stupid one. The next morning I snapped at my adviser and said I was dropping the branch. A week later, in the canteen, I actually looked at my marks. I had passed every other subject. One paper. And what I was running from was not the branch. It was everyone seeing me fail. I had nearly changed my whole life to hide from a feeling.

Urmila: Did you send the form?

Vasudev: No. But I had to go back and apologise to my adviser first.

qa.q: What did Vasudev find on looking at the marks a week later?
qa.a: Vasudev had passed every other subject, with only one paper failed.

qa.q: What was Vasudev feeling when filling in the transfer form?
qa.a: Vasudev felt ashamed and angry, thinking everyone had seen the failure.

qa.q: What could Vasudev have done on the night of the result?
qa.a: Vasudev could have waited a few days, looked at all the marks and talked with the adviser before any big decision.

qa.q: How might the adviser have felt when snapped at?
qa.a: The adviser may have felt surprised and concerned, until Vasudev came back to apologise.

grounding: Shows Vasudev deciding in anger and shame to drop the branch and later seeing the choice was driven by the feeling.

subtype: Approach: names the feeling, waits, and then plans [Revision]
passage:
At four, with the client report due at nine the next morning, Tenzin stared at seventeen open tabs. Her chest felt tight. She put her hands flat on the desk and said quietly, "I feel anxious."

Lalremsiami looked up from the next desk. "Want some tea?"

"A walk," said Tenzin. She went down the stairs and around the block twice, counting the trees on the way. When she came back she opened a blank page and wrote down everything that still needed doing: seven items. She starred the three that the client would read first and put a time beside each. The other four went under "if time". The tabs closed one by one. It was still a heavy evening, but the pressure had a shape now.

qa.q: How many items did Tenzin write down as still needing doing?
qa.a: Tenzin wrote down everything that still needed doing: seven items.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when she said "I feel anxious"?
qa.a: Tenzin felt anxious and overwhelmed, with a tight chest and many tabs open.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do if the three starred items still take too long?
qa.a: Tenzin could ask the client or Lalremsiami about priorities, or trim what the report covers.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami see Tenzin's walk?
qa.a: Lalremsiami may feel concerned but respectful, having offered tea and accepted the walk instead.

grounding: Shows a person naming anxiety about a deadline, taking a walk and sorting tasks into a short list.
